title: Cross off a label, pour the shelf
allegory: A tensor is a pantry of jars on labelled shelves; reduce is a new floor plan with a label crossed off, so every jar along that shelf is poured together into one, and the last word on the plan says how to pour.
map: shelf labels on the door plan
axis names in the pattern string
a label crossed off the new plan
an axis missing from the output: it is the one reduced over
how you pour: blend, tip it all in, keep the fullest
fewer jars come out, and you cannot un-pour
the element count shrinks; reduce is not invertible

chapters.name: The average picture
chapters.note: arr.mean(0) ... or was the batch axis 1?

cap.1: You have eight pictures and want one average picture. Old code does it with a bare axis number, and nothing says which axis you just averaged away.
cap.2: arr.mean(axis=0) runs, but is axis 0 the batch or the colour? Pick the wrong one and you still get a picture, just the wrong picture.
cap.3: Positional reductions like mean(dim=k) name the vanishing axis by index. Nothing checks that index against intent, so the wrong reduction still returns a well-formed tensor.

cap.1: Same pantry as before. Now you cross a label off the plan on the door, and every jar along that shelf is poured together into one. Fewer jars come out.
cap.2: reduce reads the same pattern string as rearrange. Any axis on the left that is missing on the right is the axis it reduces over.
cap.3: reduce(x, 'b h w -> h w', 'mean') averages over b. Axes absent from the output are reduced; the kept axes can be regrouped exactly as in rearrange, all in one validated pattern.

cap.1: Left of the arrow: the shelves now. Right: the shelves you keep. Every label you leave out gets poured. The last word says how to pour.
cap.2: 'b c h w -> b c', 'mean' averages over height and width, leaving one number per image per channel. That is global average pooling in one line.
cap.3: Output axes are kept; input-only axes (h, w) are reduced with the named op: 'mean', 'sum', 'max', 'min' or 'prod'. Composite input axes give pooling: (h h2) with h2=2 and 'max' is a 2x2 max-pool.

cap.1: Two shelves of three jars. Cross off w and each shelf pours into one jar: 1, 2, 3 blend to 2, and 4, 5, 6 blend to 5. Six jars become two.
cap.2: Shape (2, 3) goes to (2,). The count shrinks from 6 to 2, the one thing rearrange can never do. Mean gives [2, 5]; sum would give [6, 15].
cap.3: Output size is the product of the kept axes only. Each output cell is many-to-one, so unlike rearrange it cannot be inverted: repeat can copy [2, 5] back out, not restore the six values.

cap.1: One shelf, three ways to pour. Blend to the average: 2. Tip it all into one jar: 6. Keep only the fullest jar: 3.
cap.2: The third argument picks the reduction. Sum grows with the length of the axis you drop; mean does not. That is why losses are usually averaged over the batch.
cap.3: sum scales with the reduced axis length, so a summed loss has a batch-size-dependent gradient; mean is length-invariant. max passes gradient only to the argmax element.

chapters.name: Which label, exactly

left.title: 'b c h w -> c h w'

right.title: 'b c h w -> b h w'

chapters.verdict: The label you cross off decides what gets blended. Read it before you run it.

cap.1: Cross off the wrong label and you still get pictures. One pour blends eight pictures into one; the other quietly turns every picture grey.
cap.2: Both patterns run. With bare numbers, mean(0) versus mean(1) is a one-character difference; with names, the difference reads as b versus c.
cap.3: A reduction over the wrong axis yields a valid tensor, and when two axis sizes coincide even the shape agrees. A named pattern puts the reduced axis in the source, where review can see it.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Global average pooling at the end of a ResNet
Averaging a loss over batch and positions

cap.1: You will pour shelves constantly: squashing an image to one vector, averaging a loss, finding a model's typical activation to compare against.
cap.2: ResNets end with 'b c h w -> b c', 'mean'. Losses average over batch and sequence. Interpretability starts from mean activations over a dataset.
cap.3: Mean activations over a reference distribution underpin mean-ablation and difference-of-means steering vectors: reading and steering a model starts with choosing the right reduction.

caption.1: Tap jars to add to them. Watch each pour: shelf averages, column maxes, one grand total. Notice how few jars are left.
caption.2: Tap one jar many times: its column max jumps once it is the fullest, its shelf mean creeps up by a quarter per tap, and the total rises by exactly your taps.
caption.3: Each reduction hears a change differently: sum passes it through (gradient 1), mean divides it by the axis length (1/n), max ignores it unless that element is the argmax.

hamming.what: A named-axis mean, sum or max: the axes missing from the output are the ones collapsed.
hamming.when: Whenever you pool an image, average a loss, or summarise activations across a batch.
hamming.why: Naming the collapsed axis makes the reduction readable and checkable, and since it cannot be undone you want it right first time.

object.title: The pouring rack
object.subtitle: Twelve jars on three shelves; cross off a label and whole rows pour into one.

knobs.label: Cross off: none (0), w (1) or h (2)

cap.1: Twelve jars on three shelves, each filled to its own level.
cap.2: A (3, 4) tensor. Bar height is the value in each cell.
cap.3: Input x with shape (h=3, w=4); heights are the raw values.

cap.1: Cross off w. Each shelf pours into its first jar and the rest stand empty: three jars left.
cap.2: 'h w -> h', 'mean': shape (3, 4) becomes (3,). Each remaining bar is its row's average.
cap.3: out[i] = mean over j of x[i, j]. The element count drops from 12 to 3.

cap.1: Same label crossed off, a different pour: keep only the fullest jar on each shelf.
cap.2: 'h w -> h', 'max'. The middle shelf jumps to 1.2 because one jar dominates it.
cap.3: max selects one element per row, so a gradient would flow to that argmax alone.

cap.1: Cross off h instead. Now each column pours toward the front shelf: four jars left.
cap.2: 'h w -> w', 'mean': (3, 4) becomes (4,). Which label you drop decides the answer.
cap.3: Reducing over h gives out[j] = mean over i of x[i, j]: a different axis, a different tensor.

cap.1: From above: three full jars, nine empty. Could you refill the nine from the three? No. Pouring forgets.
cap.2: repeat can copy a poured value back along the shelf, but the original levels are gone.
cap.3: reduce is many-to-one and not invertible; repeat(reduce(x)) is a broadcast of the summary, not x.

predict.q: You cross off w from 'h w' on this rack. How many jars are left?
predict.why: Every jar along w pours together, leaving one jar per h. Crossing off h instead would leave 4.

predict.q: A shelf is poured with 'sum', then made twice as long with similar jars. The poured jar:
predict.why: sum grows with how many jars you pour; mean does not. That is why losses are usually averaged over the batch.

predict.q: After a reduce, can repeat bring the original jars back?

options.t: No, it only copies the poured value back out

predict.why: reduce throws information away; rearrange and repeat never do.
